units: the training space is laid out as four separate stations
the opening station is where raw stock is sorted and cleaned
marking out calls for careful checking so that assembly does not go wrong
the assembly step uses clamping tools worked by two people
the final station brings together sanding, finishing and checking of measurements
a posted sheet gives the order of operations, the tolerances allowed and the safety gear
the instructor moves around to correct how the students handle their hands
you have to go through every station before you are allowed to work unsupervised
text: A hands-on training workshop breaks down into four stations, and each one covers its own family of movements. The opening station handles raw stock: the apprentice weighs, sorts and cleans whatever will pass through later. At the second, everything is marked out, and careful checking of those marks heads off costly trouble at assembly. Third comes the bench, fitted with vises, clamps and a screw press that two students work together. The last station, which most people find tedious, brings together sanding, finishing and measuring to spec. A sheet pinned to the wall lists the order of operations, the tolerances allowed and the protective gear required. The instructor moves from bench to bench, adjusting a grip here, straightening a shoulder there. Every student passes through all four stations before earning the right to work unsupervised.

units: teaching happened first through watching an elder and repeating
the arrival of writing froze the procedures into books
moving pictures later promised a clearer explanation
the writer disputes the idea that this sequence is steady progress
each medium gains in reach what it loses in human presence
the written book reaches distant readers but corrects no movement
the moving image shows a movement from every angle without sensing the hesitation of the person watching
the conclusion argued for is that no medium replaces the presence of an elder
text: Once, teaching was almost wholly a matter of imitation. The learner watched an elder, copied, failed and began again. Then writing arrived and locked the procedures into manuals, turning something alive into something dry. Screens came later and promised clarity of a fresh kind: animated diagrams, explanations cut into steps, a smooth path forward. I would argue that this sequence is no ascent at all. Every medium has gained in reach exactly what it has given up in presence. A manual reaches readers the workshop would never have taken in, yet it cannot steady a shaking hand. Moving pictures show a movement from every angle and never once feel the hesitation of whoever sits watching them. The conclusion takes few words: no medium stands in for an elder leaning over unfinished work.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: an injury to her hand marked the start of her path
she had to work out unusual grips to hold her tools
that constraint made her alert to how each person handles an instrument
she built a reputation as a very fine teacher
she breaks every movement into steps for beginners
her workshop took in students who had been turned away elsewhere
she cut back her own output in order to teach more
that choice lowered her income
her former students, now experts, still use her method
text: The bookbinder in question lost the use of two fingers while she was still young, and that injury shaped the whole course of what came after. She could not hold the folder the way her classmates did, so she was forced to work out grips of her own, and that made her alert to the way other people take hold of a tool. The same alertness later earned her a reputation as a superb teacher. Since she had broken every movement down into steps to make it possible for herself, she could break down a beginner's clumsy attempt just as readily. Her workshop drew students whom other workshops had turned away at the door. As demand grew, she cut back her own output and gave her afternoons over to teaching. The choice cost her income, but it spread: her former students, seasoned now, still work by her method.

units: the beginner's manual is irritating from the opening pages
the author piles up definitions and breaks off his demonstrations with digressions
the reader finishes a chapter without being able to name what he took in
the content itself is judged to be good
the criticism bears on the arrangement and not on the substance
reading it in reverse, starting with the exercises, cleared up the difficulty
the exercises are graded and honest about how hard they are
the book then becomes a resource where you look for what is missing
the advice is to open the theory only when you get stuck
text: Honestly, this beginner's manual annoyed me from the very opening pages. It is a tangle. The author piles up definitions, doubles back on himself, drops a digression into the middle of a proof. You finish a chapter unable to say what you picked up. Worst of all, the material itself is good; it is just served in a jumble. So I tried something: read the thing backwards, starting with the exercises. That cleared everything up. The exercises are superb, graded, honest about how hard they get. Work them first and you find out what you lack, then go hunting for the definition that is missing. The book turns into a store you draw from rather than a corridor you get pushed down. So yes, I would recommend it, with one instruction: start at the back, and open the theory only once you are stuck.

units: the writer reports on two training courses taken during the same term
the first gathered a large group in a tiered lecture room
the speaker there talked without being interrupted
the second brought a very small number together around a table
the woman running the second fell silent as soon as a question came up between participants
the first covered a wide syllabus and left the participants passive
the second moved more slowly and drew out exchanges
a newcomer there got further than a seasoned practitioner
the writer recommends the second arrangement despite its narrower syllabus
text: Dear colleague, here is the account I promised of the two courses I sat through this term, since they contradict each other point for point. The first packed a good thirty of us into a tiered lecture room: the speaker talked, we took notes, and nobody broke in. The second gathered a handful of us around one table, and the woman running it fell silent the moment a question passed between us. The first covered a wide syllabus and left us diligent but idle. The second inched along and made us talkative, muddled at times. Where the first rewarded a tidy page of notes, the second rewarded a mistake said out loud. A newcomer got further there than a seasoned practitioner, because he dared admit what he had not followed. If you must pick for the team, take the second, even at the cost of ground covered.

units: a student asks a stoneworker what learning is
the answer comes as an ordered list
the first item is accepting dullness
the movement made endlessly is compared to water wearing away rock
the second item is accepting difficulty
an obstacle overcome leaves a mark that ease does not leave
the third item is taking account of what the material will allow
another item is putting up with harsh correction from an elder
the last item is forgetting what was learned so that the hand comes before thought
the craftsman refuses to put a number on how long it takes
text: What does it mean to learn? The student puts the question to the stonecutter, who answers with a list, the way a man lays out his tools along a bench. To learn, he says, is first to consent to dullness: a movement made endlessly wears its way in as water wears limestone. It is next to accept what is hard, not from any taste for pain, but because an obstacle beaten leaves a mark that ease will never press. It is to listen to the stone, which refuses one curve and asks instead for another. It is to bear the eye of an elder who corrects without comforting. It is at last to forget what was learned, so that the hand moves ahead of the mind. How many seasons, the student asks, does that road take? The stonecutter smiles, wipes his chisel and says such a span is crossed, never counted.

units: the instructor first asks for the power to the device to be cut
the trainee reports that the indicator light keeps blinking
the instructor explains that a residual charge stays in the capacitor
you have to wait for that charge to drain away
the cover comes off by loosening the screws crosswise
uneven tightening warps the sealing gasket
the trainee then measures a residual voltage of nothing
the instructor requires the operation to be logged in a register before reassembly
the procedure only holds good if every step is dated and signed
text: The instructor began by telling the trainee to cut the power to the device and watch for the indicator light to go out. She answered that it was still blinking. He explained that a residual charge lingers in the capacitor and that you have to wait until it has drained away entirely. Next he had her take off the cover, loosening the screws crosswise rather than one after another around the rim. She asked what lay behind that rule. Uneven tightening warps the sealing gasket, he told her. She then measured the residual voltage and reported a reading of nothing at all. The instructor accepted the measurement and had her log the operation in the register before anything went back together. He finished by saying the procedure is worthless unless every step is dated and signed.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the spread of town workshops changed the way trades were taught
families were no longer enough to supply the hands needed
masters took children from elsewhere into their own homes
living together this way gave rise to written agreements
the agreements set the term, the upkeep and the secrecy
the ban on teaching outside the workshop protected the worth of the trade
that ban held back the spread of technique
the guilds never settled the contradiction between secrecy and renewing the workforce
travelling workers carried the skills from one workshop to another
text: As workshops multiplied in the towns, the passing on of a trade changed in kind. Families could no longer supply the hands that were wanted, so masters began taking children from elsewhere into their own homes. Living under one roof led to written agreements: how long the bond would run, what food was owed, which methods were never to leave the premises. Secrecy guarded the worth of the trade, so teaching outside the workshop was forbidden, and that ban slowed the spread of technique. Out of it came a contradiction the guilds never managed to settle, since guarding a method meant starving the trade of fresh arms. When traffic between regions picked up, travelling workers carried the skills from one workshop to the next all the same. Secrecy gave way through movement, then, not through any decision of the masters.

units: material read again feels familiar and that familiarity is mistaken for command of it
the student thinks he is ready and then finds himself helpless later on
recognizing a statement takes less effort than producing it from memory
the brain confuses these two sensations
the answer is to question yourself without looking at your notes
the effort of recall strengthens memory even when it fails
the recalls have to be spaced further and further apart
the spacing stretches to the point where forgetting becomes likely
this method leaves a feeling of failure although it works
text: Anyone studying alone runs into a familiar trap: material read a second time feels familiar, and that feeling passes for command of it. The reader shuts his notebook confident, then finds himself helpless a week later. The mechanism is well established. Recognizing a statement costs less effort than producing it from memory, and the brain mistakes one sensation for the other. The fix is a reversal. Instead of rereading, you ask yourself the question and hunt for the answer with your notes shut. The effort of recall strengthens the trace far better than a pleasant reread does, even when nothing comes. You then space those recalls out, close together at first, wider and wider after that, up to the point where forgetting starts to threaten. The method feels thankless, because it makes you feel unsuccessful while it works.

units: the narrator showed the same knot to two learners
the younger one got it after a single demonstration and two failed tries
she asked no questions
the grown man listened closely and took notes
he questioned the narrator about the logic of the crossing
he did not get the knot all evening
the man was trying to understand where the young one simply copied
the narrator took his notebook away and covered his eyes
the man succeeded quickly once he could not see
the narrator concludes that his explanations got in the way of the man's hands
text: I taught the same knot to two learners last season, and the comparison has been nagging at me ever since. The younger one needed a single demonstration: she grabbed the rope, botched it twice running, then got it right without my saying a word, and without asking me a single question. Her neighbor, a grown man, listened to me with perfect courtesy, took notes, asked sharp questions about why the crossing works the way it does. And he failed at it the whole evening. It was not that he learned worse; he learned differently, wanting to understand first what the girl was content to copy. When I finally took his notebook away and tied a cloth over his eyes, his hands found the answer in three tries. The lesson stings a little: my explanations had fed his head and frozen his fingers.
